title: Gulf Allies' Frustration With Trump Deepens Over Iran War Fallout
excerpt: Persian Gulf states face growing disillusionment with Washington after being left exposed to Iranian missile and drone attacks during a conflict they did not start and could not control.
body:
• Gulf allies say they were not given adequate warning before U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered retaliatory attacks across the region
  • Iran launched at least 380 missiles and over 1,480 drones at Gulf countries since the conflict began, according to an AP tally
  • The emerging U.S.-Iran agreement grants Tehran a formal role overseeing Strait of Hormuz traffic, alarming Gulf states
  • Some Gulf nations are now exploring alternative military suppliers, including Turkey, as confidence in U.S. security guarantees erodes

The relationship between the United States and its Persian Gulf allies has entered its most strained period in decades, with governments across the region voicing deep frustration over Washington's handling of the Iran conflict and the emerging agreement that may reshape the region's security architecture.

Officials from two Gulf countries told the Associated Press their governments were disappointed with how the U.S. handled the early stages of the war, particularly the initial strike on Iran on February 28. They were not given advance notice of the U.S.-Israeli attack, despite having previously warned Washington that such action could trigger severe consequences.

A Region Under Fire

The consequences were swift and devastating. Iran launched at least 380 missiles and more than 1,480 drones at Gulf countries since the conflict began, according to an AP tally based on official statements. Six U.S. soldiers were killed in Kuwait when an Iranian drone struck an operations center at a civilian port. Drone strikes also targeted U.S. diplomatic facilities in Riyadh and Dubai.

"From the Arab Gulf states' perspective, the Iran war is a disastrous turning point for the regional security order."

— Hasan Alhasan, Senior Fellow, International Institute for Strategic Studies

One official told the AP there was frustration — and even anger — among Gulf governments that the U.S. military response focused primarily on protecting Israel and American troops, leaving Gulf countries largely to defend themselves.

A Deal That Deepens Unease

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio toured the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait in late June, stressing that Washington would not "undermine" its Gulf allies in negotiations with Iran. But the emerging agreement has done little to reassure the region, according to CNN.

The pact grants Iran a formal role in overseeing commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz alongside Oman — meaning much of the Gulf states' maritime trade and energy exports could be conducted under Iranian oversight. It fails to address Iran's missile program or its network of proxy militant groups, which many Gulf states consider more urgent threats than Tehran's nuclear activities.

Trump appeared to downplay the missile issue, saying it was "only fair" for Iran to have missiles if Saudi Arabia does. The deal also envisions a $300 billion reconstruction fund for Iran, which Trump committed Gulf funding toward — though Saudi Arabia has said it has "no details" about the proposal.

Rethinking Alliances

Some Gulf states are already looking to diversify their military procurement, particularly by turning to Turkey as an alternative supplier of arms, a senior Gulf diplomat told CNN. Officials are increasingly contemplating a future where Washington plays a much smaller role in regional security.

"America as a strategic ally that can be relied upon is now very much in question in the Gulf states."

— Firas Maksad, Managing Director, Eurasia Group (Middle East and North Africa)

The Wall Street Journal reported that Gulf states were left questioning how hard Washington would push for a deal that protects America's friends, after Trump went from threatening that "a whole civilization will die tonight" to accepting Iran's 10-point demands within hours.

What's Next

Despite the frustration, Gulf states recognize they have few alternatives. The UAE's diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash told reporters the country would "double down" on its U.S. relationship, even as trust erodes. For Indian Americans and the broader diaspora with economic ties to the Gulf, the shifting security dynamics could have implications for business operations and energy markets across the region.

The immediate question is whether the cease-fire holds and whether formal negotiations produce a deal that addresses Gulf concerns — or leaves America's oldest Middle Eastern partners feeling abandoned.
